cards.explanation: The answer is that Pharaoh will say they're lost and boxed in. The LORD tells Moses, Israel's leader, what Pharaoh, king of Egypt, will say: “They are wandering the land in confusion; the wilderness has boxed them in.” So Pharaoh will see a people with nowhere to go. It's like watching a driver circle the same block and assuming they have no clue. The LORD already knew what He was doing, and He told Moses ahead of time.

The answer is “know.” God says the Egyptians “…will know that I am the LORD.” He says it again in verse 18, when He talks about being honored through Pharaoh, his chariots, and his horsemen. That's the same promise twice, so I'd say He wants it heard, friends. Pharaoh had brought a whole army, and God still said it plainly.

The answer is that they say they released Israel from serving them. Pharaoh and his officials say, “We have released Israel from serving us.” The people who did the work are gone, and now they're counting what that costs them. It's the sound of a boss who just noticed the empty desks.

The answer is False. Pharaoh “…took 600 of the best chariots, and all the other chariots of Egypt, with officers over all of them.” So the 600 were the best of the bunch, and the rest came along too. Every chariot of Egypt was in that line. That's a lot of chariots for one chase.

The answer is that they cry out to the LORD in terror. The Israelites “…were terrified and cried out to the LORD.” They looked up, saw the Egyptians marching after them, and their first move was to call out to Him. I'd say that's a good first move, friends, even with the fear.

The answer is True. The people really say it: “…it would have been better for us to serve the Egyptians than to die in the wilderness.” They also remind Moses of what they'd said back in Egypt: “Leave us alone…” I think fear can make even slavery sound like the easy option. Moses answers in the next verse: “Do not be afraid.”

The answer is True. Moses says, “for the Egyptians you see today, you will never see again.” That's a big promise to make with an army in sight. He says it right after telling them the LORD's salvation comes today. Stay tuned, friends, because the sea will show what he means.

The answers are “fight” and “still.” Moses says, “The LORD will fight for you…” Israel isn't asked to win this one. The battle belongs to the LORD, and that's the comfort. Moses also says, “you need only to be still.” The people had been crying out and complaining, so being still was a big ask. Their job in that moment was to stand there and let the LORD work.

The answer is that Moses is to stretch his hand out over the sea to divide it. The LORD says, “…lift up your staff and stretch out your hand over the sea and divide it…” Moses's part is to lift the staff and stretch out his hand. The LORD does the rest. A very simple instruction for a very big sea.

The answer is “dry.” God says the Israelites can “…go through the sea on dry ground.” The text says it again in verses 22 and 29, so it's worth noticing. Dry ground, with walls of water on the right and on the left. I'd have rubbed my eyes twice.

The answer is True. The angel of God, who had gone before the camp, went behind them, and the pillar of cloud stood behind them too. The text says it “…came between the camps of Egypt and Israel.” So the cloud sat right between the two camps. And “…all night long neither camp went near the other.”

The answer is False. The cloud “…came between the camps of Egypt and Israel,” and “…all night long neither camp went near the other.” The army wasn't closing in. The cloud stood between them, lighting the night.

The answer is a strong east wind. “…all that night the LORD drove back the sea with a strong east wind that turned it into dry land.” The wind blew all night long. Then the waters were divided, and the Israelites went through on dry ground. My chef's hat would not have survived that night, friends.

The answer is “water.” The Israelites went through “…with walls of water on their right and on their left.” The text says it in verse 22 and again in verse 29. It's quite a hallway. Water on both sides, dry ground in the middle.

The answer is “wheels.” The LORD “…caused their chariot wheels to wobble, so that they had difficulty driving.” Wobbly wheels are something anyone who has pushed a shopping cart can picture. Right after that, the Egyptians say, “…the LORD is fighting for them against Egypt!” The wheels were the problem, and the Egyptians noticed who was behind it.

The answer is True. The Egyptians say, “Let us flee from the Israelites, for the LORD is fighting for them against Egypt!” That's the Egyptians themselves saying it. It's the same thing Moses told Israel in 14:14. Even the army could see what was happening.

The answer is not one of them. The waters covered the chariots and horsemen, “…the entire army of Pharaoh that had chased the Israelites into the sea. Not one of them survived.” This is a heavy part of the story, friends. The text is plain about it, so I'll be plain too.

The answer is that they fear the LORD and believe in Him and Moses. The people “…feared the LORD and believed in Him and in His servant Moses.” They had just seen His great power over the Egyptians. After all that crying out and complaining, they believed. I love that.

The answer is that the LORD has thrown horse and rider into the sea. The song says, “The horse and rider He has thrown into the sea.” That's the first thing it celebrates. Moses and the Israelites sing it right after crossing.

The answer is True. The song says, “He is my God, and I will praise Him, my father’s God, and I will exalt Him.” So the song praises Him as the God of the singer's father too. It reaches back to the family before him. It's a short line with a lot of history.

The answer is the LORD's right hand. The song says, “Your right hand, O LORD, has shattered the enemy.” Notice the song stops talking about Him and starts talking straight to Him. The line right before it calls that hand “…majestic in power…” The words right hand show up twice in one verse, so the song really wants us to look at His hand.

The answer is the blast of the LORD's nostrils. The song says, “At the blast of Your nostrils the waters piled up…” It's a picture of His power in the way a poem would put it. The currents stood firm “like a wall…”

The answer is “sea.” The song says, “But You blew with Your breath, and the sea covered them.” The enemy had bragged about what they would do. The sea answers it. They “…sank like lead in the mighty waters.”

The answer is False. The song asks, “Who among the gods is like You, O LORD?” and then, “Who is like You—majestic in holiness, revered with praises, performing wonders?” The song asks it as a question with no one to name. So no god is on His level.

The answer is to His holy dwelling. The LORD leads the people He has redeemed, and the song names the goal: “…Your holy dwelling.” I think that tells us the journey doesn't end at the sea. Verse 17 adds more, calling it the mountain of His inheritance and the sanctuary His hands have established. That's where the song is headed.

The answer is False. The song says, “The nations will hear and tremble…” and that anguish will grip Philistia. Edom's chiefs will be dismayed and Moab's leaders will be seized with trembling. No welcome party in sight.
The answer is “reign.” The song ends, “The LORD will reign forever and ever!” It's a big finish after a big song, friends. It doesn't end with Egypt or the sea, it ends with Him.

The answer is all the women. The text says Miriam the prophetess, Aaron's sister, “…took a tambourine in her hand, and all the women followed her with tambourines and dancing.” So the women are the ones who follow her. Then Miriam sings back to them. That's a lot of tambourines.
